title: Jaundice on tuberculosis treatment — recognise the danger and explain the immediate plan

blocks.text: Jaundice on tuberculosis treatment — recognise the danger and explain the immediate plan

Round 5 • PACES Station 2: acute consultation • Skills C communication, E clinical judgement, F managing concerns, G welfare (with focused A/B/D where relevant) • 20 minutes • Educational examiner-style encounter • Prepared 14 October 2026 • Not an official PACES mark scheme

A 45-year-old receiving standard treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis has developed anorexia, nausea, yellow eyes and dark urine. Assess likely treatment-related harm and explain safe changes to their regimen.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: Hook: Suspected anti-tuberculosis drug-induced liver injury from hepatotoxic first-line agents; alternative hepatic causes still need testing. Trap: Do not continue hepatotoxic drugs despite symptomatic significant ALT rise; equally do not abandon TB treatment without a specialist regimen, susceptibility and infection-control plan.

rows: “First I need to check if this is affecting your immediate safety.”
“I have a working diagnosis but need to exclude dangerous alternatives.”
Viral hepatitis, biliary obstruction, alcohol-related liver disease and other hepatotoxic medicines must be considered.
These symptoms may mean liver inflammation caused by TB medicines. We need to hold the liver-toxic medicines now, check your clotting and involve your TB team urgently.

Urgently contact treating TB service; stop potentially hepatotoxic TB drugs when ALT ≥3× ULN with symptoms or ≥5× without symptoms, and assess clinically. Check INR, bilirubin, ALT, AST and other causes; specialist TB team devises non-hepatotoxic cover if required and supervises sequential reintroduction after recovery.
Your tuberculosis still needs effective treatment. The specialist team will plan temporary cover if needed and carefully reintroduce drugs when safe.
Check patient priorities, understanding and follow-up.

blocks.text: Opening line: “The TB tablets are making me yellow. Can I simply stop everything for good? Will the infection come back?” The actor is concerned but able to engage unless the examiner introduces deterioration. Release only history in the candidate brief; do not volunteer a diagnostic label. Ask “Why do you need to do that?” after proposed treatment. Acknowledge clear, compassionate explanations.

R2/R3: Missing the characteristic pattern or treating a suggested cause as proven. Viral hepatitis, biliary obstruction, alcohol-related liver disease and other hepatotoxic medicines must be considered.

R4/R5: Omitting the named critical action. Do not continue hepatotoxic drugs despite symptomatic significant ALT rise; equally do not abandon TB treatment without a specialist regimen, susceptibility and infection-control plan.
R6: Saying “we will monitor” without a comprehensible explanation of what is being done.
“I will check whether this patient is physiologically unstable before proceeding.”

“The key safety issue is: Do not continue hepatotoxic drugs despite symptomatic significant ALT rise; equally do not abandon TB treatment without a specialist regimen, susceptibility and infection-control plan.”
“Let me explain why the next investigation and treatment cannot wait.”

True jaundice during anti-tuberculosis therapy is not the same as expected orange/red body fluids caused by rifampicin. New clinical jaundice requires urgent liver injury assessment, including INR and severity signs, and rapid discussion with the TB team about interrupting hepatotoxic drugs. Avoid advising the patient to restart implicated drugs independently; TB specialist and hepatology teams determine safe treatment alternatives and reintroduction.

THINK: Suspected anti-tuberculosis drug-induced liver injury from hepatotoxic first-line agents; alternative hepatic causes still need testing. SAY: These symptoms may mean liver inflammation caused by TB medicines. We need to hold the liver-toxic medicines now, check your clotting and involve your TB team urgently. DO: Urgently contact treating TB service; stop potentially hepatotoxic TB drugs when ALT ≥3× ULN with symptoms or ≥5× without symptoms, and assess clinically. Check INR, bilirubin, ALT, AST and other causes; specialist TB team devises non-hepatotoxic cover if required and supervises sequential reintroduction after recovery. NUMBERS: 20-minute encounter. TRAP: Do not continue hepatotoxic drugs despite symptomatic significant ALT rise; equally do not abandon TB treatment without a specialist regimen, susceptibility and infection-control plan. FINISH: Your tuberculosis still needs effective treatment. The specialist team will plan temporary cover if needed and carefully reintroduce drugs when safe.

ATS/CDC/IDSA drug-susceptible tuberculosis guideline, 2016 — https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/treatment-of-drug-susceptible-tb/ — supports treatment/urgency decisions; accessed 14 October 2026.
